hook.text: Electric cars had every advantage in 1900 except two: range and refueling speed.

buildup.text: Early electrics managed about 30 miles per charge. A tank of gas could go ten times farther.

discovery.text: Oil discoveries in Texas made gasoline dirt cheap. Electricity outside cities was nearly nonexistent.

twist.text: Charles Kettering's electric starter in 1912 removed the hand-crank—gas cars' biggest drawback.

climax.text: By 1920, gas stations dotted every road. Charging stations wouldn't return for almost 100 years.

punchline.text: Gasoline didn't win on technology. It won on infrastructure.

quiz.question: What invention removed gas cars' biggest user complaint?

details.summary: Gasoline defeated electric cars by 1920 through a combination of higher energy density, cheap oil, expanding road networks, Ford's affordable Model T, and the invention of the electric starter motor that eliminated hand-cranking.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding gasoline's victory reveals that it was not inevitable. Specific historical events and economic forces, not inherent technological superiority, determined a century of petroleum-powered transportation.
takeaways: Gasoline has roughly 80 times the energy density of lead-acid batteries
Cheap Texas oil made fuel far more affordable than electricity per mile
The electric starter motor removed gas cars' biggest usability disadvantage

faq.question: Was gasoline always cheaper than electricity for driving?
faq.answer: Not initially. In the early 1900s, electricity was competitive in cities. But the 1901 Spindletop oil gusher in Texas crashed petroleum prices, making gasoline dramatically cheaper per mile for the expanding road network.

faq.question: Could better batteries have changed the outcome?
faq.answer: Possibly. If rechargeable batteries with even a fraction of gasoline's energy density had existed, the energy cost advantage of oil might not have mattered as much. But that level of battery technology took another century to develop.
